Issued at 328 AM CDT Fri Aug 7 2026

Through Saturday:

In spite of a steady stream of cirrus over our southeastern CWA
and patchy mid-level clouds farther to the northwest, light 
winds and plenty of near-surface moisture (surface dew points 
ranging from the mid 60s to low 70s) has allowed for fog to 
develop in some spots within our forecast area. At the time of 
this writing, most of the noteworthy visibility reductions 
being reported at area ASOS/AWOS sites have been focused across
our southeastern counties near and beneath the cirrus canopy, 
interestingly enough. In fact, a few observation sites there 
have already reported 1/4 mile visibility, and with conditions 
not expected to start improving until after sunset, have went 
ahead and issued a Dense Fog Advisory for roughly the 
southeastern half of our forecast area this morning. It's 
possible that this advisory may need to be expanded northward as
radiation fog gets a greater foothold in areas where skies are 
comparatively clearer, so we'll be monitoring observational 
trends closely the rest of the night.

One other thing we'll be monitoring through this morning is an 
arc of convection that sprouted near and east of St. Louis
earlier along the nose of a ~35 kt southwesterly low-level jet.
This low-level jet is progged to veer more westerly with time, 
and this may tend to steer the associated convection more 
towards the east, which would keep most or all of it just south
of our area. That said, the 00Z run of the FV3, which appears 
to be the only convection-allowing model that has a relatively 
good handle on the ongoing convection (I suppose the saying 
about a blind squirrel finding a nut every now and then would 
apply here), doesn't veer this low-level jet as much as other 
guidance does and brings this convection into our southern 
counties towards sunrise as a result. Have thus maintained some 
chance PoPs and lower-end thunderstorm chances for the 
southern/southeastern third or so of our CWA through this 
morning to cover this possibility. Otherwise, the majority of 
the area should remain dry through this afternoon with high 
temperatures today reaching the low-mid 80s.

Tonight, a cold front will drop into the area from the 
northwest. There is relatively good agreement across the 
spectrum of the latest hi-res guidance that convection will be 
ongoing along the front by midday today in southern 
Minnesota/northern Iowa, but model solutions then diverge in how
this convection evolves thereafter. Would think that the 
frontal forcing, augmented by lift provided by an upper-level 
shortwave and upper-level divergence in the left exit region of 
a northwesterly 70-80 kt jet, should generate enough convection 
for a consolidated cold pool to eventually materialize
somewhere. This cold pool would then drive the associated 
convective complex towards the east and/or southeast through
this afternoon and into this evening. Depending on exactly 
where along the front this potential MCS develops, this scenario
could put northern Illinois in this MCS's crosshairs this 
evening with some threat for strong to locally damaging winds 
before the complex weakens with time. On the other hand, if no 
real organized convective complex takes shape upstream of our 
area, or if the thunderstorm cluster follows a sharper 
southeastward or even southward propagation (like a few CAMs are
suggesting), then our area could miss out on storms and even 
precipitation altogether tonight as the aforementioned cold 
front works its way through the area. Upstream convective trends
will thus need to be monitored closely this morning and 
afternoon, but for now, have nudged our PoP and thunderstorm 
chances up a bit from what they were previously.

The cold front should stall out somewhere in or near our 
southern CWA Saturday morning. Humid conditions with low 70s 
dew points will persist south of wherever the front sets up, 
while more comfortable air will be found north of the front. 
High temperatures on both sides of the front are favored to end 
up in the 80s again, though weak onshore flow into northwest 
Indiana and part of Cook County will likely keep temperatures in
the mid-upper 70s in areas immediately downwind of Lake 
Michigan. While the air mass along and south of the stalled 
frontal boundary will be unstable enough to conditionally be
supportive of thunderstorms, limited surface convergence along 
the front, essentially no upper-level forcing support, and weak 
capping all point towards the daytime hours on Saturday 
remaining dry across our forecast area.

Ogorek

unchanged as a strengthening upper ridge in the southwest CONUS 
will amplify the northwest flow over the Great Lakes. As a 
result, periods of thunderstorms are expected to traverse across
